unfinished on another. The repeat is dropped, and its done flag goes
with it, so the tally loads as unfinished and saves that way.

Storage.describe reads as wording, and copies the damaged file aside
partway through. Its own comment says a method that describes something
should not change the disk.

Let's have the task that is kept take the done flag of any copy
carrying it, and move the copying up to load, which is where the
decision about damage already lives, leaving describe with nothing to
do but word what happened.

Of the two readings, done is the one that cannot be recovered by
looking at the file afterwards.

The plan covers both of this week's console changes, which it did not:
an event whose dated ends run backwards, and a file naming a task
twice.

Also here:

* The README lists only two of the six increments done with AI.
* parseEvent, Event's constructor and LoadResult document a program
  that refused less than this one does.
* One symbolic-link test still builds its link by hand, which is what
  linkOrSkip was pulled out for.
* Four method names are not verbs: withoutByteOrderMark,
  withoutDoneFlag, asList, and a test helper called consoleReading.
* Two tests have no blank line before them.
* The atomic rename falls back on too narrow an exception.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge review-round-two into master
Hold every road into a task to the same spacing
commitResults.messageBody:
Tally treats runs of spaces inside a description as insignificant, so
"read    book" and "read book" are the same task and the second is
refused. The parser does that tidying, and the data file reader does
not, so the file is a way around a rule the keyboard enforces:

    T | 0 | read    book
    T | 1 | read book

loads as two tasks, on a tally no command could have produced.

Let's tidy the spacing where a task is made rather than where a command
is read, so the rule holds however the task arrived. The parser has
nothing left to do about it.

The plan covers the last two console changes that had only unit tests
behind them: a command typed in capitals, and a data file an editor
marked as UTF-8. The mark is written into the plan as <BOM> rather than
as itself, so nothing in the plan is invisible, and the case adds a
task so the file is written back without it.

Also here:

* Reading a repeat searches the tasks twice, once to find that there is
  one and once to mark it done.
* linkOrSkip counts any IOException as a file system without symbolic
  links, so a link that fails because something already sits at the
  name is reported as an environment rather than as the fault it is.
* Event says its ends are kept exactly as typed, readTally documents
  only half of what it returns, and two test helpers are named without
  saying they stand in for the process's own streams.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge review-round-three into master
Read an event's dates from the ends it keeps
commitResults.messageBody:
An event tidies the spacing of its two ends and then reads its dates
from the text it was handed rather than from the text it kept. The list
shows an event carrying two readable dates while the free-day search
steps over it and reports that the answer left events out.

The same reading lets a padded pair past the check for ends that run
backwards. The file loads, saving writes it back tidied, and the next
start refuses the very line it accepted a moment ago.

Let's read the dates from the ends the event keeps.

That alone moves the fault rather than fixing it: the parser and the
reader ask the question of the untidied text, so a padded pair slips
past them and reaches an assertion that stops the program. Let's put
the question itself in one place, taking the ends as written and
tidying them where it is answered, so everyone asking gets the answer
the event would give.

Also here:

* linkOrSkip counts almost any FileSystemException as a file system
  without symbolic links, which hides a broken fixture. It now asks
  once, with a link of its own, and lets real failures fail.
* Event still describes its ends as raw, exact, and as the user typed
  them.
* One test has no blank line before it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge fix-event-dates into master
Cover padded dates, and credit the test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
The fix for an event reading its dates from the wrong text changes what
Tally prints for a stored event whose dates are padded, and the plan
says nothing about it. TC-35 covers the same rule at the keyboard,
where the padding never survives to be a problem.

Let's add the case at the file's side: an event the list shows and the
free-day search counts, and a padded pair running backwards that the
reader refuses as it would refuse an unpadded one.

The padding sits in front of each date rather than behind it. A space
at the end of a line in the plan is invisible, and an editor that trims
it would break the case without anyone touching the program.

The plan credits itself to Claude in its own header, and the README's
list of what Claude wrote leaves it out. Let's name it there too.

Also here: three comments and one aim still say an event's ends are
kept exactly as typed, and two tests have no blank line before them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge review-round-four into master
test plan: Name the line the backwards pair is on
commitResults.messageBody:
TC-39 says the file's third line pads a pair of dates that run
backwards. It is the second, which is what the warning the case expects
says, so the case passes while its own reasoning points at the wrong
line.

Let's say the second.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge fix-plan-typo into master
docs: Point the download at the release it means
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide sends the reader to the releases page and leaves them to pick
one. There is a release to name now.

Let's link v0.3, so the jar the guide describes is the jar they get.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split storage, and name a boolean as one
commitResults.messageBody:
The course's code quality script flags two things.

Command holds its boolean as changesTally, where the standard asks for
a name that sounds like a boolean: isSet, hasData, canEvaluate.

Storage runs to 614 lines and does three jobs: it reads the data file's
format, it replaces a file without risking what is in it, and it
decides what either of those calls for.

Let's rename the boolean to canChangeTally, and give the first two jobs
classes of their own, TaskLine and FileReplacer. Neither knows anything
about the other, and Storage decides without knowing how either is
done.

Storage is 365 lines now. The tests follow the same seam: the questions
about the format are asked of TaskLine directly, where they need no
file at all, and StorageTest keeps the ones about what happens to one.
Coverage outside the window is unchanged at 98%.

The script's third flag, on a field's header comment, is a false
positive it warns about. The standard scopes the "Returns ..." form to
method header comments, and the example it gives for a class member is
a noun phrase like the one flagged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge quality-feedback into master
Give the last two jobs classes of their own
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage still keeps the damage aside and decides afterwards whether
writing is allowed, and it holds the state that decision leaves behind.
Tally still works out how every reply about the tally reads, alongside
deciding what happens and when it is said.

Let's move both out, into Quarantine and Replies.

Storage is 273 lines, from 614 before any of this. Tally is 334, from
450. By code rather than by line the two are smaller still, at 132 and
167: more than half of every file here is the Javadoc the standard
asks for, which is why the size of a class and the size of its job are
worth counting separately.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge storage-quarantine into master
TaskLine: Answer an unreadable line with Optional
commitResults.messageBody:
read returns the task a line stands for, or null when the line is no
task at all. Every caller has to remember that, and one that forgets
hears nothing about it until the null reaches somewhere far from here.

Let's answer with an Optional, so the absence is part of what read says
rather than something to know about it.

The helpers behind it still pass null among themselves, which read
keeps to itself: they sit a few lines apart and are read by whoever is
reading read.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split the storage tests by what they ask about
commitResults.messageBody:
StorageTest holds the tests for what a data file is made of and the
tests for what happens to one. They are two subjects, and reading
either means passing over the other.

Let's put them in files of their own, and give the symbolic link they
both need a helper of its own rather than a copy each.

Only whether links can be made at all is worth skipping a test over.
That question is asked once, with a link of its own, so that a link
refused for any other reason fails as the fault it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Separate a command word on tabs as well as spaces
commitResults.messageBody:
A task's own text has its spacing tidied wherever it comes from, so a
tab inside a description is recorded as a space. The command word is
split off on a literal space alone, so the same line typed with a tab
after the command is refused as a command nobody knows.

Let's separate the two on any run of spaces or tabs.

The plan spells a tab as <TAB>, beside the <BOM> it already spells out.
A plan holding a real one holds something nobody can see, and an editor
that tidied it away would break a case without anyone touching the
program.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Say why the JAR runs without -ea
commitResults.messageBody:
Assertions are on for the app run through Gradle and for the tests, and
off in the JAR people download. Read from here that looks like an
oversight rather than a choice.

Let's write the reason beside the flag: an assertion states something
this code believes about itself, and the answer to one turning out
false is a stack trace for whoever is working on it, not a crash in
front of whoever is using it. What a user types is checked by the
parser and what a file holds by the reader, and neither leans on
assertions being on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Task: Name the date pattern in the usual terms
commitResults.messageBody:
The comment on the date pattern opens by calling it the one shape a
date may be written in, which says what it is for before saying what it
is.

Let's name the syntax it holds, and leave the paragraph below to say
why the pattern exists at all.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge review-round-five into master
Keep what the file system said about a failure
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage turns an IOException into a TallyException carrying words the
user can act on, and drops the exception it came from. TallyException
has nowhere to put one. Whoever is working out why a file would not
open is left with a sentence written for somebody else.

Let's give TallyException a constructor that takes the cause, and hand
it the IOException. The user reads the same words as before, and the
reason is there for whoever needs it.

commitResults.messageTitle: README: Run the jar from where the build writes it
commitResults.messageBody:
The build writes the jar to build/libs, and the line under it runs
tally.jar from the repository root, where no such file is. Anyone
following the two commands in order meets an error.

Let's name the path the build just printed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge release-and-causes into master
docs: Point the download at the newest release
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide links v0.3, and the jar there answers a command typed with a
tab after it as a command nobody knows. v0.4 carries that fix and the
ones after it.

Let's link v0.4, so the jar the guide describes is the jar they get.

commitResults.messageTitle: Flatten how the loading note is put together
commitResults.messageBody:
The note about a data file is built in a nest: the sentence saying
writing is refused sits inside the branch for lines that could not be
read, so the reader has to hold one condition in mind to see when the
other applies.

It need not. The only refusal that reaches this method comes from a
copy that could not be made, and no copy is attempted unless a line
could not be read, so the two always arrive together.

Let's put the three sentences side by side, one condition each, and say
in a comment why the middle one can stand where it does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge flatten-note into master
Name the value that scrolls to the newest message
commitResults.messageBody:
The conversation is scrolled by setting a bare 1.0, which says nothing
about what it means. A scroll pane measures its position from 0 at the
top to 1 at the foot, so the number is a place rather than a distance,
and the line reads as neither.

Let's name it, and say in the comment what the scale is.

A comment added with the last change also left a trailing space, which
the style check refuses. Let's take it off.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge name-scroll-value into master
Note the goodbye rather than answering it back
commitResults.messageBody:
runCommand returns a boolean, and its name says nothing about which of
the two means what. Both callers read it as if (!runCommand(line)),
where the reader has to work out that false is the goodbye. The field
that records the goodbye already exists, and both callers read it a
moment later anyway.

Let's set that field where the goodbye is carried out, and let
runCommand return nothing. The loop that reads commands drops a branch,
and the window is told the farewell only by the command that earned it.

Also here:

* The window scrolls to 1.0, which is only what a scroll pane happens
  to call its foot until someone sets a different maximum. It asks the
  pane instead, and the constant naming the literal goes with it.
* Two assertions compare against a boolean literal where the assertion
  named for it says the same thing in fewer words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge predicate-and-vmax into master
Say the farewell where the goodbye is carried out
commitResults.messageBody:
getResponse keeps a second flag beside the first. isExiting records
that the user has said goodbye and stays true; wasExiting records
whether it was already true a moment ago, so that the farewell goes to
the command that earned it and not to every command a window sends
afterwards.

That is a rule the caller has to reconstruct from two flags, for
something the command itself knows.

Let's say the farewell where the goodbye is carried out, alongside
every other reply that command gives, and leave run to add one only
when the loop ended without a goodbye, which is what happens when the
input runs out instead.

Typing bye a second time is now answered a second time, where the old
pair of flags let it pass in silence. A command that asks to leave is
better answered than ignored, and the window stops taking input at the
first one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge say-goodbye-once into master
Hold the second goodbye to being answered
commitResults.messageBody:
The last change decided that bye asked twice is answered twice, where
the pair of flags it replaced let the second pass in silence. Nothing
in the suite sends bye twice, so the decision rests on the commit
message alone, and the next person to tidy that branch would not hear
about it.

Let's send it twice and expect both answers.

None of the four tests already about the goodbye notices when the
second one is swallowed again; this is the only one that does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge test-repeated-bye into master
Point the download at the newest release
commitResults.messageBody:
The guide links v0.4, and the jar there was built before the last ten
commits. v0.5 carries them.

Let's link v0.5, so the jar the guide describes is the jar they get.
